text: The model works. Now comes the part that decides whether anyone notices: checking your work, being honest about limits, cleaning up, and presenting the project.

Review each criterion from the kickoff, with evidence. A U C of point seven nine eight beats the point seven five gate, so that passes. Recall by plan was reported, and it exposed weak weekly plans. And say plainly what you never verified: a real endpoint, permissions, and real latency.
Here is the weak segment. At a single threshold of point five, recall on weekly plans was only sixteen percent. Overall recall was fifty-six percent, which hid it.

One lever is the threshold. I picked a threshold per plan on the validation set, then applied it to the untouched test set. Overall recall rose to seventy-three percent, but precision fell from seventy-one to sixty-one percent. We catch more churners, and we call more customers who would have stayed. Whether that pays off is a business decision.

Ship the project with a model card covering the data, metrics, limits, and what the model must not be used for. Then clean up. Delete the monitoring schedule, the endpoint, its config, and the model. Confirm in billing that nothing still accrues, and keep a budget alert on.

For the five-minute walkthrough, state the problem and criteria, show the architecture on one slide, then the results, including the weak segment, and what you would do next with real data and a real account. Candor about limits impresses reviewers more than claiming perfection.

That completes the AWS Data Science course. You have gone from S3 and IAM, through SageMaker training, tuning, and pipelines, to deploying, monitoring, and costing a model. Next in the Data Scientist path is Machine Learning Operations for Data Scientists, where you automate what you did by hand here.
